context: operational-readiness-led · turnout/alerting systems & apparatus-bay fit-out set the pace

brief.intro: New to this project type? A fire or civil-defence station is mostly a straightforward low-rise building — apparatus bays for the trucks, a drill tower, dormitories, admin and training space — but its acceptance criteria are operational, not just architectural. The turnout/alerting system has to get crews suited and rolling within seconds of a call, vehicle-exhaust extraction has to protect health inside the bays, and standby power has to change over automatically so the station never goes dark mid-response. The building shell is rarely the constraint; the heavy-duty apparatus-bay slab/drainage/exhaust fit-out and the specialist alerting-system commissioning are.

scope.name: Enabling & site works
scope.desc: Earthworks, yard drainage and drill-tower foundations.

scope.name: Structure & apparatus bays
scope.desc: Structural frame, heavy-duty bay slab designed for repeated vehicle loading, and dormitory/admin floors.

scope.name: Envelope & apparatus-bay doors
scope.desc: Roof, walls and fast-acting apparatus-bay doors sized for the turnout time target.

scope.name: Electrical power
scope.desc: Normal and standby distribution with an automatic transfer switch (ATS) changeover.

scope.name: HVAC & vehicle-exhaust extraction
scope.desc: Ventilation and comfort cooling, plus a captured hose-reel/rail system removing diesel exhaust from the bays.

scope.name: Plumbing
scope.desc: Domestic water and drainage, including an oil/water interceptor for bay wash-down.

scope.name: Fire & life safety
scope.desc: Fire alarm and sprinkler protection for the building itself, not the operational firefighting scope.

scope.name: Alerting / turnout systems
scope.desc: Station alerting (tones, lighting, PA) tied to the dispatch centre, and locker/route layout designed around turnout time.

scope.name: Testing & commissioning
scope.desc: Alerting-system proving, vehicle-exhaust test, standby-power changeover test and drill-tower proving.

glossary.plain: the garage where fire trucks/appliances are parked, ready to roll.
the sequence from alarm to truck leaving the bay — the whole station design is built around cutting this time.
the tone/light/PA system that wakes and directs crew the instant a call comes in, tied to the dispatch centre.
a captured hose-reel/rail system that removes diesel exhaust from the bay instead of venting it into the building.
a purpose-built training structure for rope, ladder and rescue drills.
the automatic transfer switch to generator power so the station never loses power mid-response.
the layout of gear lockers and routes designed to minimise the seconds firefighters take to suit up.

must_get_right: The alerting/turnout system, not the building shell, is the true acceptance test — protect real commissioning time for it.
Apparatus-bay slab, drainage and vehicle-exhaust extraction are heavy-duty, specialist fit-out items — don't schedule the bay as a generic garage.
Prove the standby-power changeover live, under load, before handover — a station that goes dark mid-response has failed its core purpose.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities carry durations in working days; the network is calculated (F9) with no artificial constraints beyond contractual milestones. Total float is kept ≥ 0 in the baseline.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Civil and structure run a standard 6-day calendar; the apparatus-bay slab and heavy-duty finishes follow standard concrete cure/finish durations; alerting-system commissioning and the live turnout drill are scheduled on the same shift pattern the station will actually operate under.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The driving path runs apparatus-bay slab & structure → vehicle-exhaust & bay fit-out → alerting-system rough-in → dispatch-centre tie-in → live turnout-drill proving → standby-power changeover test → handover. The dormitory/admin fit-out is rarely on the critical path.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Design is frozen and authority approvals (building and fire/civil-defence operational approval) obtained per phase gate; the dispatch centre and its interface protocol are confirmed before alerting-system design is finalised; a single mobilisation. Any change to these invalidates the baseline dates.

sections.heading: Procurement & long-lead items
sections.body: The schedule is driven by a small number of specialist procurement items. The following are tracked as milestones and drive the network:

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Apparatus-bay slab and door installation require clear yard access and coordinated concrete/steel deliveries; alerting-system and dispatch-tie-in commissioning depend on a scarce, specialist integrator resource; if the existing station remains operational during works, phased handover of bays is a major sequencing constraint.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks: dispatch-centre interface delays, alerting-system integration debugging, and re-tests of the standby-power changeover under load. Schedule contingency is held immediately before the live turnout-drill proving and again before final handover, rather than spread thinly across the network.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the field — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
